power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The target sample size was determined a priori using G*Power, based on the correlation between OC scores and choice accuracy in the exploratory study (ρ=-0.2, p=0.03); a power analysis targeting 95% power at α=0.05 yielded N=313, and data collection stopped once this target was reached. Ethical approval was granted by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (15/LO/1361); all participants gave informed consent.

No OC-related effect reversed in direction relative to the online study. The nonreplication of the OC performance correlations and s-PE model is most plausibly attributable to insufficient statistical power: the fMRI cohort is approximately five times smaller than the online sample, and the expected effect sizes (ρ≈-0.10 to -0.20) require N≥100-150 to reach α=0.05 with adequate power. The replication of the ab-PE×OC interaction (the strongest and most theoretically central finding of the online study) across both timepoints provides direct behavioural support for the neuroimaging analyses that follow. We therefore interpret the fMRI behavioural data as confirming the key prediction-error-based mechanism linking OC traits to impaired structural updating, while acknowledging that the smaller sample was insufficient to detect the weaker correlational effects observed in the online cohort.

live_data_statements: To dissociate three candidate mechanisms of cognitive inflexibility: (i) the initial formation of stimulus-outcome associative beliefs, (ii) the updating of those beliefs following unsignalled structural changes, and (iii) the ability to infer unobserved but structurally related associations in the absence of direct feedback, we developed a novel structural inference task and administered it to a large general-population online sample recruited via Prolific with a preregistered design (N=313; UK-based; aged 18-45 years; 39.6% female; M=32, SD=6.7; see Methods for exclusion criteria).

On each trial, participants were shown a rocket and made four sequential accept/reject judgements, one for each rocket-product (RP) pair, about whether that product was associated with the rocket, testing their knowledge of the full top-to-bottom chain (Figure 1c).
The remaining two were no-feedback (no-FB) rockets, where no outcome was shown and participants had to rely on their internally updated structural model to make correct predictions.
Participants were told that such changes could occur at either level, but not when.
After the experiment, participants completed a set of psychiatric questionnaires.
Only one change occurred at a time, and participants were informed of this possibility, but not of the time when they might occur.

We first confirmed that participants were able to use their structural knowledge to make correct predictions, with performance clearly above chance across all choice trials, even when including the transient below-chance dip that follows a structural change by design (one-sample t-test vs.
Participants completed two practice phases and a comprehension check before the main experiment (Figure 1a; see also Methods).
Participants were required to answer all correctly before proceeding; an incorrect answer prompted repetition of the full question set.
Critically, high OC participants completed significantly fewer structural changes than those with low OC scores (ρ=-0.144, p=0.011; Figure 4a).
Participants were more likely to switch after an ab-PE; however, ab-PE was integrated less in participants with higher OC scores, resulting in greater choice repetition.
Participants were recruited via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/); eligibility was restricted to UK-based individuals aged 18-45 years.
A total of 432 participants enrolled in the confirmatory study.
Ethical approval was granted by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (15/LO/1361); all participants gave informed consent.
Participants completed 14 MBs in the main experiment.

There were two types of change: two rockets swapped positions between structures, or two products swapped positions (Figure 1e); only one change occurred at a time, and participants were informed of this.

Before proceeding, participants completed multiple-choice comprehension questions on the structural hierarchy, FB/no-FB distinctions, and change rules; all had to be answered correctly, with errors triggering repetition of the full question set.

After the main task, participants completed a questionnaire battery: the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) 27, Short Scales for Measuring Schizotypy (SSMS) 57, Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS) 25, Apathy Motivation Index (AMI) 26, Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) 58, Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale-42 (DASS-42) 24, Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS) 59, and the International Cognitive Ability Resource (ICAR) 28.
Participants were compensated £8.00/hour plus a performance-dependent bonus (£0-£2), with partial compensation of £4.50 for incomplete sessions.
The study received approval from the UCL Research Ethics Committee (14261/002), and all participants gave informed consent.

This behavioural sample was larger than the neuroimaging sample (N=51), as eight participants were excluded from imaging analyses due to excessive movement (Ν=6) or imaging artefacts (Ν=2) but retained for behavioural analyses.

text.text: Impaired cognitive flexibility, the ability to form and update latent structural associations, is a hallmark of psychiatric conditions such as obsessive-compulsive (OC) disorder, yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

Using a novel structural inference task, we dissociated three candidate mechanisms: (i) initial acquisition of associative structures, (ii) belief updating following structural changes, and (iii) inference about unobserved associations.

In a large general-population sample (N=313), transdiagnostically characterised OC symptoms were linked to impaired updating following structural change and reduced generalisation to unobserved associations, whilst initial learning remained intact.

Using fMRI (N=51), we found this was driven by overrepresenting structurally irrelevant associations in medial orbitofrontal cortex, and impaired formation of novel latent associations in posterior hippocampus.

These findings reveal that OC-related cognitive inflexibility is grounded in dissociable fronto-hippocampal representational failures that impair structural model revision, rather than the capacity to acquire latent associations in the first place.

To dissociate three candidate mechanisms of cognitive inflexibility: (i) the initial formation of stimulus-outcome associative beliefs, (ii) the updating of those beliefs following unsignalled structural changes, and (iii) the ability to infer unobserved but structurally related associations in the absence of direct feedback, we developed a novel structural inference task and administered it to a large general-population online sample recruited via Prolific with a preregistered design (N=313; UK-based; aged 18-45 years; 39.6% female; M=32, SD=6.7; see Methods for exclusion criteria).

The task required participants to learn two parallel hierarchical structures, each spanning three levels: rockets at the top were linked to planets in the middle, which were each associated with two out of four possible products at the bottom (Figure 1b).

text.text: On each trial, participants were shown a rocket and made four sequential accept/reject judgements, one for each rocket-product (RP) pair, about whether that product was associated with the rocket, testing their knowledge of the full top-to-bottom chain (Figure 1c).

The remaining two were no-feedback (no-FB) rockets, where no outcome was shown and participants had to rely on their internally updated structural model to make correct predictions.

We have thus developed a novel structural inference task that teases apart the formation, flexible updating, and generalization of latent structural associations.

Using a large-scale online study, we found that obsessive-compulsive (OC) traits were linked to impoverished updating of latent associations following structural change, and to a corresponding failure to generalize these updated associations to unobserved, inferred associations, whilst initial latent structural learning remained intact.

text.text: To characterise the underlying mechanism, we tested whether OC-related performance differences could be explained by weaker integration of explicit prediction errors to update associative beliefs.

Using a logistic random intercept model, focused only on trials where feedback was given, we predicted whether participants changed their accept/reject choice on a given RP pair, relative to their previous encounter with the same pair, as a function of the associative-belief prediction error (ab-PE) on that prior encounter, a binary signal coding whether feedback had shown their choice for that pair to be wrong (1) or right (0).

The associative-belief prediction error (ab-PE) is a binary signal coding whether feedback on the same pair in MBt contradicted the participant's choice (ab-PE=1) or confirmed it (ab-PE=0).
Participants were more likely to switch after an ab-PE; however, ab-PE was integrated less in participants with higher OC scores, resulting in greater choice repetition.

These results indicate that slower performance recovery after structural change reflects decreased integration of pair-level feedback signals to revise individual associative beliefs and redirect behaviour.

To probe structural neural representations independently of choice behaviour, we introduced fMRI suppression blocks (SBs) interleaved with the task's choice blocks (CBs) (the imaging equivalent of the online mini-blocks), in which participants made the same FB and no-FB rocket-product judgements described above.

In SBs, all possible stimulus pairs were presented in rapid succession and pseudorandom order, without a behavioural response, allowing representational strength to be measured independently of choice.

This leveraged the principle of repetition suppression: the more strongly two stimuli are associated, the more their neural co-occurrence suppresses the regional response, providing an implicit, behaviour-independent measure of representational strength relative to unassociated pairs 30, 31 .

Cognitive flexibility depends on forming and updating latent structural associations.

Using a novel task, we found that obsessive-compulsive (OC) traits impair structural processing selectively at later stages: initial learning was intact, but higher OC scores were linked to diminished integration of evidence after structural change and reduced sensitivity to structural prediction errors during inference, mirrored by increased mOFC representation of irrelevant associations and reduced hippocampal representation of novel associations.
These findings identify altered structural-representation adaptation, not basic associative learning, as a core mechanism of OC-related cognitive inflexibility.
Earlier studies often blur initial learning with subsequent rule updating, making it difficult to isolate where OC-related deficits occur 12, 13, 35 .

text.text: By separating these phases, we found high-OC individuals performed as well as others on comprehension checks and pre-change trials, echoing prior evidence that OCD individuals accurately learn initial associations before contingency changes 15, 36, 37 , and ruling out generalised explanations such as attentional deficits or degraded associative encoding.

text.text: Together, this suggests that OC-related inflexibility is not a general deficit in learning or updating, but emerges specifically when relational structures must be revised.
Indeed, OC-related deficits only emerged after a structural change: high-OC individuals completed fewer changes and recovered more poorly, despite comparable performance in stable periods.

Trial-level analysis attributed this to reduced sensitivity to associative-belief prediction errors, i.e. reduced revision after disconfirmatory feedback, consistent with Bayesian accounts linking OCD to impaired response to contingency shifts 44, 45 and broader reversal-learning alterations 12, 40, 46, 47 .

text.text: Reduced sensitivity to structural prediction errors in OC individuals was also found to drive the impaired generalization to unobserved associations.
This hints at a broader impoverishment of internal models.

Whilst both hint at a common mechanism, individuals greatly differed in the impact of prediction errors on these two separate behaviours (Supplementary Note 3), suggesting that high-OC individuals may be heterogeneous, with some showing one of the two prediction-error deficits but not necessarily both.
Neurally, these prediction-error deficits were mirrored in structural representations.
In high-OC individuals, mOFC, a selective encoder of hidden task states 4, 32, 50 that normally holds a consolidated store of stable relational structure 29 , over-represented irrelevant pairs.

text.text: Together, these results refine existing accounts of OC-related cognitive inflexibility.

Compulsivity has classically been characterised as reliance on habit systems due to impaired goal-directed control [15] [16] [17] 36 , stemming from impoverished internal-model representations 18, 56 .

text.text: Our results clarify that this impoverishment reflects not a basic failure to acquire the model but an impaired capacity to calibrate it under structural uncertainty, so rigidity is most pronounced in post-change, evidence-sparse, inference-dependent contexts.
Extending this paradigm to clinically diagnosed OCD samples is an important next step.
In sum, OC-related cognitive inflexibility reflects not a failure of control or learning capacity but a representational precision issue that compounds when structural demands are highest.

Fronto-hippocampal circuits supporting structural model maintenance and revision emerge as a mechanistic target for understanding and addressing the inflexibility characterising OCD and related disorders.

text.text: The structural inference task dissociated three components of structural behaviour: initial formation of associative beliefs, updating after unsignalled change, and inference about unobserved associations without direct feedback.
Participants learned two parallel hierarchical structures (rockets-planets-products) and made sequential rocket-product predictions.
A subset of trials provided explicit feedback (enabling direct belief updating), while the remainder withheld feedback, requiring reliance on the internally maintained model.
Unsignalled structural changes required detecting change from feedback evidence and propagating updated knowledge to untested associations.
Points were awarded for correct choices and converted into a monetary bonus.
The task comprised two parallel three-level hierarchical structures: a rocket linked to a planet, each planet associated with two of four possible products (Figure 1b).
text.formatted: The task comprised two parallel three-level hierarchical structures: a rocket linked to a planet, each planet associated with two of four possible products (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: On each trial, participants viewed a rocket and made four sequential accept/reject judgements about candidate products (Figure 1c); 'accept' indicated a belief that the rocketproduct pair (RP) belonged to the same structure.

text.text: Each rocket was permanently assigned to a feedback (FB) or no-feedback (no-FB) condition.
On FB trials, the two correct products were revealed after choices, alongside points awarded; on no-FB trials, a fixation cross appeared instead.

Because the two structures are fully interconnected (including anti-correlational associations between rockets and products from different structures), FB-trial information can in principle be used to infer correct no-FB associations, requiring participants to maintain and deploy an updated internal model.
Points from both trial types contributed to the performance bonus.
Choice trials were organised into mini-blocks (MBs; Figure 1d).
text.formatted: Choice trials were organised into mini-blocks (MBs; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1d</ref>).

text.text: Each MB comprised 20 trials: four rockets × four products, plus one unanalysed planet-predictor trial (no feedback).
Rocket order was randomised within condition; the two FB rockets always preceded the two no-FB rockets, ensuring complete structural information was available before no-FB inference.
Because each MB probed the full set of associations, beliefs could be quantified directly from trial-level choices without computational modelling.
Participants completed 14 MBs in the main experiment.
Structural changes were triggered when participants exceeded 70% FB accuracy (Figure 1d, dotted line).

text.text: To prevent anticipation, a change occurred with 50% probability at threshold crossing; if not triggered, it was forced at the next crossing.
A minimum of two MBs separated successive changes (except the first, permitted after MB 1, since both structures had already been instructed).
The maximum number of changes was six (constrained by trial count); the minimum was one.

There were two types of change: two rockets swapped positions between structures, or two products swapped positions (Figure 1e); only one change occurred at a time, and participants were informed of this.

text.text: Swaps always involved either two FB rockets or one FB and one no-FB rocket (never two no-FB rockets), preserving complete structural inferability.
Change-type order (rockets vs. products) was fixed across participants; the number of changes experienced was performance-dependent.

During the instruction phase, participants viewed an explicit display of the task's hierarchical structure and learned the stimulus-level assignments (Figure 1b), encoded via a card-matching game in which structures were shown with items missing and participants selected correct completions from six options.

text.text: Before proceeding, participants completed multiple-choice comprehension questions on the structural hierarchy, FB/no-FB distinctions, and change rules; all had to be answered correctly, with errors triggering repetition of the full question set.
Participants then completed two practice phases, each containing one structural change: the first with FB trials only, the second alternating FB and no-FB trials as in the main task.
Each phase comprised 3-5 MBs; participants needed 50% FB accuracy by the fourth MB, or were shown the full structure and given one further MB to reach threshold, else excluded.
The main-task threshold was 70%; criteria were disclosed to participants beforehand.

text.text: The study lasted approximately 80 minutes.
Participants were compensated £8.00/hour plus a performance-dependent bonus (£0-£2), with partial compensation of £4.50 for incomplete sessions.
Performance was measured as choice accuracy, assessed across the entire experiment (Figure 2a), separately for FB and no-FB trials, and time-locked to structural changes.

text.text: Because the experiment was structured into MBs, we compared performance in the MB before the change (MBt-1, reflecting participants' maximum FB accuracy), the MB during the change (MBt), and the subsequent MB (MBt+1, reflecting performance recovery once full structural information was available).
These timepoints were of particular interest for comparing the formation of associative beliefs (MBt-1) against belief updating following new feedback (MBt+1).
Reaction times were recorded but not reported, as uncontrolled variability from online testing (hardware, browser rendering, network latency) rendered them unsuitable for meaningful inference.

We used a transdiagnostic approach to define latent psychiatric dimensions across seven questionnaires (Supplementary Figure S3) 16 , applying factor analysis to 22 subscales while accounting for intra-and inter-questionnaire correlations.

text.text: The number of latent factors was determined via the Catell-Nelson-Gorusch (CNG) scree test on eigenvalues (Supplementary Figure S3b) 60 .

text.text: The first factor was labelled anxious-depressive, the second social unease, and the third (our factor of interest) obsessivecompulsive.
Factor scores were used to relate individual differences to structural acquisition, belief updating, and inference.
The same set of questionnaires was used across both exploratory and confirmatory study, while the reported results show a replication of factor classification.
We used two logistic random-intercept models to quantify how evidence integration drove behavioural change on FB and no-FB trials.

The first tested whether explicit action-outcome evidence (FB trials) updated associative beliefs; the second tested whether structural evidence observed on FB trials informed inference about unobserved but structurally related associations (no-FB trials).
Separating these models allowed us to dissociate belief updating from inference over latent associations.

We tested the degree to which evidence was integrated to update associative beliefs and direct behavioural change (Figure 4d-e), focusing on FB trials, which capture explicit stimulus-outcome updates.
text.formatted: We tested the degree to which evidence was integrated to update associative beliefs and direct behavioural change (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4d-e</ref>), focusing on FB trials, which capture explicit stimulus-outcome updates.

text.text: We used a logistic random-intercept model predicting trial-wise switch (=1) or stay (=0) decisions for the current pair relative to the previous encounter of the same pair, with a random intercept for subject ID.

Stay/switch was predicted by: (a) associative-belief prediction error (ab-PE): whether the choice on the previous encounter of the same pair was incorrect (1) or correct (0), (b) obsessive-compulsive trait (OC) scores: derived from the previous factor analysis, (c) and the interaction between both variables, ab-PExOC.
Regressors were normalised (mean = 0, SD = 1) within person; OC scores were normalised across participants.
The interaction effect quantified how ab-PE integration changed with OC severity.
Model: switch ~ ab-PE + OC + ab-PE×OC + (1|subject).
Choices for the first predictor within each mini-block were included, ensuring belief updating had not yet occurred via feedback within that block.

Next, we tested whether structural information from FB trials, indicative of potential change, informed inference about related but unobserved associations on no-FB trials, using the same logistic random-intercept approach (trial-wise switch/stay for both no-FB predictors, random intercept for subject ID).

Stay/switch was predicted by (a) structural prediction error (s-PE): 1 -mean accuracy on the FB trials preceding the no-FB trials within the same MB, so that a higher coefficient reflects a stronger impact of s-PE on switching, (b) obsessive-compulsive (OC) scores: derived from the previous factor analysis, (c) changed pair: whether the current no-FB pair had itself changed at the most recent structural change, together with all interactions between s-PE, changed pair and OC (s-PE×changed pair×OC).
Regressors were normalised as above.
Inference analyses included participants who experienced more than one structural change (N=303), ensuring at least one postchange inference window.
The interaction effect quantified how s-PE integration changed with OC severity.
The model was refined by restricting s-PE to FB pairs that had changed relative to the prior structural change, testing whether the most relevant information was underused on inference trials.
Models: switch ~ s-PE×changed pair×OC + (1|subject), and switch ~ sPE_change×OC + (1|subject).

The pre-registration specified separate prediction errors for changed-structure (sPE_change) and same-structure (sPE_NOchange) pairs; entered simultaneously, the OC interaction was specific to sPE_change (β=-0.056, z=-3.51, p<0.001), with no interaction for sPE_NOchange (β=-0.005, z=-0.33, p=0.743), justifying the focus on sPE_change.

Non-significant correlations were complemented with Bayesian analyses to distinguish inconclusive results from evidence for the null.
All analyses were repeated on the neuroimaging behavioural dataset (Supplementary Note 1).
A neuroimaging study (Study 2) was conducted in an independent sample to investigate the neural representations underlying the behavioural components identified online.

Study 2 characterises how these components are instantiated at the level of latent neural representations and how OC-dimension differences relate to representational updating; primary results characterising structural formation, updating and deprecation in fronto-hippocampal networks are reported separately in a dedicated manuscript 29.

text.text: That paper focused on representational dynamics during structural learning and switching, independent of psychiatric traits, and is not reproduced here.

We instead use the same task and representational framework to address a distinct question: how OC-dimension differences modulate neural representations of structural associations, and how these relate to the online behavioural alterations.

51 neurologically and psychiatrically healthy adults participated (age=25.6±5.6 years, range 18-40; 23 male), all with normal/corrected vision and meeting MRI safety criteria, drawn from 124 online screening completers (89 eligible, 61 invited, 10 excluded before analysis: 5 inattentive, 3 technical errors, 2 excessive motion, 1 anatomical anomaly).
The study received approval from the UCL Research Ethics Committee (14261/002), and all participants gave informed consent.
The core task structure closely mirrored the online paradigm.

Participants first completed the online study; those exceeding a performance threshold (>2 structural changes successfully inferred) were invited to the MRI session, where they learned hierarchical stimulus-outcome structures and made choice-trial predictions, with some associations accompanied by feedback and others requiring inference.

text.text: Structural changes occurred without warning, requiring participants to update their beliefs.

Choice-block and structural-change procedures matched the online study: each of 14 choice blocks (CBs) presented every FB and no-FB trial once, plus a middle-layer predictor trial (20 trials/CB); unsignalled changes swapped two first-or third-layer items once FB accuracy exceeded 70%.
Participants experienced 1-6 changes (me-dian=5; all≥2).
Compared to the online study, the imaging task used novel everyday-object stimuli to avoid familiarity effects.
Explicit feedback was provided for both higher-and lowerlevel associations, ensuring sufficient information for representational updating.

The key extension was dedicated stimulus-pair presentation blocks (suppression blocks) interleaved with choice blocks, probing latent representations independently of overt decision-making: stimulus pairs were presented in rapid succession without a behavioural response, leveraging repetition suppression (reduced neural response to repeated or overlapping information reflects shared representations) 30 , similar to prior stimulus-outcome work 10 .

text.text: The logic of feedback-based learning and inference remained conceptually identical across studies.
Further paradigm details are in the Supplementary Methods.
Neural representations were operationalised at the level of pairwise stimulus associations, derived from the underlying task structure.
Stimulus pairs presented during the suppression blocks were categorised into four classes: 1.
Stable associations: stimulus pairs that belonged to the same structure both before and after a structural change.
Novel associations: stimulus pairs that became structurally related only after a structural change.
Outdated associations: stimulus pairs that were structurally related before a change but no longer valid afterwards.
Irrelevant associations: stimulus pairs that were never part of the same structure.

These categories dissociated representations that should be maintained, newly formed, or deprecated following structural change; all were defined by task structure alone, independent of participants' choices or trial-level performance.
Details of MRI data acquisition, preprocessing, and ROI definition are provided in the Supplementary Methods.
An event-related general linear model (GLM) was estimated to characterise neural responses to the different classes of stimulus pairs presented during suppression blocks.
Each stimulus pair was modelled as a single epoch regressor spanning from the onset of the first stimulus to the offset of the second stimulus.
Separate regressors were included for stable, novel, outdated, and irrelevant pairs.

Repetition suppression principles were used to index representational overlap: stimulus pairs that were jointly embedded within a latent structure were expected to evoke reduced neural responses relative to structure-irrelevant pairs.
Accordingly, the main contrasts of interest compared: • Stable vs Irrelevant pairs, • Novel vs Irrelevant pairs,
Outdated vs Irrelevant pairs.

The GLM additionally included regressors modelling task events unrelated to representational probing (predictor onset, choice phase, feedback, suppression block onset and offset), as well as motion, CSF and physiological nuisance regressors (see Supplementary Methods).
All regressors were convolved with a canonical hemodynamic response function and high-pass filtered.
Imaging data were analysed using FSL.
Subject-level contrasts were combined across runs with fixed-effects models and entered into mixed-effects group analyses.
Statistical inference used threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) with permutationbased family-wise error correction (p<0.05).

Training and initial structure learning.

Participants received a shortened recap of the online instructions and completed multiple-choice comprehension questions covering the three-layer hierarchy, the FB/no-FB mapping, and the rules governing structural changes (which layers could change; one change at a time).
All questions had to be answered correctly, with the full set repeated on any error.

Structures were then learned via a card-matching game: a partially completed diagram was shown with items missing, and participants selected the correct completion(s) from six candidates, with feedback.
A distinct, randomly generated set of everyday-object stimuli was used for each participant (never overlapping with the online session) to avoid contaminating repetition-suppression effects.
Training continued until ≥80% accuracy was reached; no participant required more than one repetition.
Trial structure (predictor phase, four binary predictor-product choices, outcome phase) followed the main Methods.
Each predictor was deterministically linked to exactly two of four products; no-FB predictors always followed sufficient FB exposure to permit inference of the full mapping.
Because each predictor belonged to only one structure, products from the other structure were implicit rejections, so no-FB choices reflected both direct knowledge and cross-structural inference.
Points were converted linearly into a monetary bonus.

Each of 14 choice blocks (CBs) presented all FB/no-FB trials once (predictor order randomised within condition; FB/no-FB block sequence fixed across participants), plus a middle-layer trial (predictor = middle node; four accept/reject judgements spanning both structures, no feedback).
Jittered intervals (gamma distribution: min 2s, max 6s, mean≈4s) preceded predictor onset, followed the choice phase, and preceded the next trial, to decorrelate BOLD responses.

At each changepoint, either two first-layer predictors or two third-layer products swapped structural assignment, constrained so that swaps always involved at least one FB stimulus (two FB predictors, or one FB + one no-FB predictor; never two no-FB predictors), guaranteeing the new structure was inferable.

The set of possible swaps was fixed across participants; timing was performance-dependent: a change became eligible once FB accuracy exceeded 70% within a CB, was implemented with 50% probability at that point (else forced at the next crossing), and was followed by ≥2 CBs before the next change was possible (except the first change, permitted after CB 1).
Participants experienced 1-6 changes (median=5, all≥2; Supplementary Fig. 2); the change sequence differed from the online task to prevent anticipation.

text.text: Each CB was followed by a Suppression Block (SB; opening/closing green fixation), presenting all 45 unordered pairs of the 10 structure stimuli as sequential two-image presentations (1.4 s/image, 0.6 s fixation), pseudorandomised so a pair's second stimulus could open the next pair (~53 images/SB), with pair order regenerated per CB and participant.
Ten astronaut catch trials per SB (appearing ≥0.5 s post-onset) required a speeded button press and contributed to the bonus, to maintain engagement.

Basic task performance was comparable to the online sample.
Participants performed above chance on both FB and no-FB trials, and FB performance was significantly higher than no-FB performance (0.914±0.014 vs.
0.887±0.020; paired t-test: t(58)=2.07, p=0.043), confirming that structural inference without feedback remained the more demanding condition.

Participants encountered a mean of 4.85±0.13 structural changes, and both FB and no-FB performance showed the expected pattern around changepoints: performance was high prior to the change (MBt-1: FB=0.977±0.006, no-FB=0.922±0.016), dropped at the change (MBt: FB=0.891±0.019, no-FB=0.870±0.023), and partially recovered in the subsequent mini-block (MBt+1: FB=0.910±0.022, no-FB=0.883±0.028; Supplementary Fig. S1a-c).

The nonreplication of the OC performance correlations and s-PE model is most plausibly attributable to insufficient statistical power: the fMRI cohort is approximately five times smaller than the online sample, and the expected effect sizes (ρ≈-0.10 to -0.20) require N≥100-150 to reach α=0.05 with adequate power.

The replication of the ab-PE×OC interaction (the strongest and most theoretically central finding of the online study) across both timepoints provides direct behavioural support for the neuroimaging analyses that follow.

We therefore interpret the fMRI behavioural data as confirming the key prediction-error-based mechanism linking OC traits to impaired structural updating, while acknowledging that the smaller sample was insufficient to detect the weaker correlational effects observed in the online cohort.

To test whether the same individuals drove both OC-related impairments, we estimated subject-level sensitivity to each prediction error signal separately.

For ab-PE sensitivity, we quantified how strongly each participant's switching behaviour on MBt+1 predictor trials was driven by the pair-level prediction error from MBt (1 -feedback accuracy on previous encounter of same pair).

For s-PE sensitivity, we quantified how strongly each participant's switch/stay decisions on no-FB trials were driven by the MB-level structural prediction error (1 -mean FB accuracy within the preceding MB).

We used two estimation approaches: (1) per-subject logistic regression betas (glmfit on each subject's trials independently), and (2) best linear unbiased predictors (BLUPs) from random-slope generalised linear mixed models (switch ~ PE + (PE|subject)), which apply partial pooling and are more stable when trial counts are low (median 16 trials/subject for ab-PE).
Spearman correlations and Bayesian correlation tests (uniform prior on ρ) 69 were used to assess the relationship between the two sensitivity measures and with OC scores.
